content: Caecitis, also referred to as typhlitis or typhlenteritis, is a condition characterized by inflammation of the cecum, which is a part of the large intestine located at the junction of the small and large intestines. This inflammation is often associated with infection. The primary cause of caecitis is the overgrowth or invasion of gram-negative enteric commensal bacteria, which are part of the normal gut flora. Among these, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most commonly implicated pathogen. Caecitis predominantly affects individuals with compromised immune systems, such as those undergoing chemotherapy, patients with AIDS, kidney transplant recipients, or elderly individuals. The clinical presentation of caecitis includes a range of symptoms such as abdominal distension, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and tenderness, and diarrhea. These symptoms can vary in severity depending on the extent of the inflammation and the patient’s overall health status. If left untreated, the inflammation associated with caecitis can extend to other parts of the gastrointestinal tract. Additionally, the cecum may become distended, leading to compromised blood supply. This ischemia, along with other contributing factors, can result in necrosis and perforation of the bowel. Such complications can lead to peritonitis (inflammation of the peritoneum) and sepsis, both of which are life-threatening conditions. The mortality rate for caecitis is alarmingly high, ranging from 40% to 50%, primarily due to its frequent association with bowel perforation. Diagnosis of caecitis is typically confirmed through imaging studies, particularly a CT scan. Radiographic findings often reveal thickening of the cecal wall and the presence of fat stranding, which indicates inflammation in the surrounding tissues.
